# Status report: jf2 allocator test on kestrel (2026-11-20)

## Short version

On a read-heavy workload, the memory allocator jf2 reduced the 99th-percentile latency of kestrel (our key-value store) by 59%. Throughput and median latency did not change beyond the variation between runs. The capacity team must still approve a memory increase of 5.7 GB (9.3%).

## Words used here

- **kestrel**: our key-value store, the program under test.
- **jemalloc**: the memory allocator library that kestrel uses now (version 5.3).
- **jf2**: our fork of jemalloc.
- **Build A**: commit 4f1c2aa of the main branch, with jemalloc 5.3.
- **Build B**: the same commit, with jf2.
- **YCSB**: Yahoo! Cloud Serving Benchmark, a standard benchmark for key-value stores. ycsb-b is its read-heavy workload. ycsb-a is its write-heavy workload.
- **p50, p99, p99.9**: latency percentiles. For example, 99% of requests finish faster than the p99 value.
- **us**: microseconds.
- **kops/s**: thousand operations per second.
- **RSS**: resident set size (the physical memory the process holds).
- **Decay purge**: the jemalloc step that returns unused memory to the operating system.
- **je_arena_decay**: the jemalloc function that runs the decay purge.
- **perf**: the Linux profiling tool.
- **Spike**: a short period of very high latency. A spike window is the time interval around one spike.
- **NUMA pinning**: binding threads to the cores and memory of one processor socket.

## Goal

kestrel shows spikes in p99 latency. The test checks if replacing jemalloc 5.3 with jf2 removes them.

## Test setup

- **Host**: bench-07, with 2 Xeon processors of 32 cores each and 512 GB of memory.
- **Kernel**: Linux 6.8.
- **System load before the runs**: load average 0.4 (almost idle for 64 cores).
- **Workload**: ycsb-b with 64 client threads.
- **Runs**: 5 per build, 10 minutes each, in alternating order (A, B, A, B, ...).
- **Reported values**: the median of the 5 runs, with the minimum and maximum.

## Results

```
Latency, median of 5 runs. One block = 250 us.

p99    A  █████████ 2140 us
       B  ███ 870 us  (-59%)

p99.9  A  ███████████████████████████████████████ 9800 us
       B  ████████████ 3100 us  (-68%)
```

Only p99 and p99.9 moved. Throughput and p50 stayed the same within the variation between runs.

| Metric | Build A (jemalloc 5.3) | Build B (jf2) | Change in median |
|---|---|---|---|
| Throughput (kops/s) | 412 (405 to 418) | 409 (401 to 415) | -3 (-0.7%) |
| p50 latency (us) | 118 (116 to 121) | 119 (117 to 121) | +1 (+0.8%) |
| p99 latency (us) | 2140 (1890 to 2610) | 870 (820 to 940) | -1270 (-59%) |
| p99.9 latency (us) | 9800 (7200 to 14100) | 3100 (2700 to 3900) | -6700 (-68%) |
| RSS at end of run (GB) | 61.2 | 66.9 | +5.7 (+9.3%) |

Each cell shows the median, then the minimum to maximum. RSS has one value per build. No range was recorded.

## What the data shows

- **p99 latency fell by 59%.** The median went from 2140 us to 870 us. Every B run was below every A run (B maximum 940 us, A minimum 1890 us).
- **p99.9 latency fell by 68%.** The median went from 9800 us to 3100 us. Every B run was below every A run (B maximum 3900 us, A minimum 7200 us).
- **Throughput and p50 did not change measurably.** The medians differ by less than 1% for both metrics. The A and B ranges overlap for both.
- **Memory use rose by 9.3%.** RSS at the end of the run went from 61.2 GB to 66.9 GB.

## Cause of the spikes

- **Timing (build A)**: the spikes occur at the same times as the decay purge.
- **Profile (build A)**: perf places 31% of the spike-window samples in je_arena_decay.
- **Build B**: jf2 runs the purge in a background thread.
- **Hypothesis**: the background purge is the reason for the lower p99 and p99.9 in build B. A perf profile of build B has not confirmed this yet. It would confirm it by showing no je_arena_decay samples in the request threads.

## Deviation from the plan

- **Event**: run 3 of build B had a 40 s stall at minute 7.
- **Cause**: the stall was traced to logrotate (the log archiving tool), started nightly by cron (the job scheduler). The allocator did not cause it.
- **Action**: the run was repeated. The results use the repeat, not the stalled run.

## Not tested

The results hold only for ycsb-b at 64 client threads without NUMA pinning. Insufficient data for these three cases:

- **ycsb-a (write-heavy)**: the run planned for 2026-11-21 covers it.
- **More than 64 client threads**: no run is in the next steps yet.
- **NUMA pinning**: no run is in the next steps yet.

## Open decision

The capacity team must decide if the RSS increase of 5.7 GB (9.3%) is acceptable.

## Next steps

1. Run ycsb-a on 2026-11-21.
2. Ask the capacity team to approve the RSS increase.
3. If they approve, enable jf2 in staging (the pre-production environment), controlled by a feature flag.

---

**Notes on this draft (not part of the report)**

- **Added by me**: the percent changes for the first four table rows, computed by hand from your medians. I also wrote "tomorrow" as 2026-11-21.
- **Assumed**: ycsb-b is read-heavy, as in the standard YCSB workload B. Correct it if your configuration differs.
- **Labeled as hypothesis**: the link between the background purge and the lower p99. Your notes have no perf profile of build B. Remove the label if you have one.
- **Gap**: your notes give no range for RSS. The report says so. Add the range if you have it.
